notes.title: What makes a neighbourhood feel walkable?
notes.body:
FIELD NOTES · 24 OCTOBER

A shaded route can feel shorter than a direct one. For our next walk, compare the experience of two streets with similar distances but very different edges.

What to notice
• Places to pause without blocking the pavement
• Shade at midday, not only in the morning
• Crossings that feel like part of the route

A question to carry forward
Does a comfortable place to stop matter as much as a clear path to keep moving?

Next step
Sketch both routes and note where each person chooses to slow down. Keep observations separate from our interpretation.

notes.title: 雨天的公共空间：观察计划
notes.body:
周三去图书馆附近走一圈。

观察雨棚、座椅和入口之间的距离。记录哪些地方让人愿意停留，哪些地方只是通行的路径。

待核查：雨天的人流变化是否与附近公交到站时间有关？

本笔记为虚构的研究示例。

notes.title: A small interview guide
notes.body:
Start with a recent experience.

“What did you notice on your way here today?”

Follow the person’s words before introducing our own categories. Leave a quiet moment after the first answer.

notes.title: Comparing heat resilience across neighbourhoods with different tree cover, building density and access to shared outdoor space
notes.body:
WORKING QUESTION

How might the same summer afternoon be experienced differently across three neighbourhoods? We should avoid treating a single temperature reading as a complete account of comfort.

Observation plan
Collect paired observations of shade, surface materials and places to rest. Note the time, recent rain and whether the route is exposed to traffic.

Evidence to seek
A public tree inventory could help us describe canopy coverage, but the age of the inventory and seasonal changes would need checking. A street map alone does not tell us whether a shaded path is accessible.

Limits
This is a fictional planning example. No measurements have been collected. We cannot infer causation from a short walk or generalise from a few interviews.

Next steps
1. Choose two contrasting routes.
2. Walk each at the same time of day.
3. Record the reasons people give for choosing a place to pause.
4. Compare notes before deciding which explanation to investigate further.

Keep questions open
Where do visitors and residents describe the same place differently? What changes when someone is carrying shopping, walking with a child, or using a mobility aid?

notes.title: One idea to revisit
notes.body: A useful map might show places to pause, as well as paths to follow.
